title: Strength Has a Bone Side: What Kind of Loading Are You Getting?
subtitle: Resistance, upright movement and balance do different jobs. Understanding the difference can make exercise choices clearer—and safer—without turning any one workout into a promise about your bones.
imageAlt: Two friends in a bright community gym: one practices a supported step-up while the other prepares to lift a pair of light dumbbells.
imageConcept: Two friends training together in a welcoming, sunlit gym, one doing a supported low step-up beside a bench while the other performs a controlled dumbbell lift; show varied ability, calm concentration and shared encouragement rather than a dramatic fitness pose.
body: “I exercise” can mean a long bike ride, a set of heavy lifts, a brisk walk, or balance practice beside a counter. All can be valuable, but they do not place the same demands on the skeleton. Muscle-strengthening work loads bone through the pull of contracting muscles; weight-bearing movement asks the body to support its weight upright; impact adds a quicker force when the feet meet the ground. Balance work has another purpose: helping you stay steady and respond to a loss of stability. These categories overlap in real life, but keeping them distinct is useful. It lets you ask not only how often you move, but what kinds of movement your week actually contains. NIAMS describes weight-bearing, resistance and balance activities as separate parts of bone-health exercise, rather than interchangeable labels [1].
The force arrives by different routes

In a resistance exercise, a muscle works against a load—such as a dumbbell, resistance band, machine or your own body weight. As the muscle pulls on its attachments, the skeleton experiences force. In a weight-bearing activity, the legs and hips help support the body against gravity while standing or moving. Walking and stair climbing are familiar examples. Hopping or jumping add impact, but that does not make them the right next step for everyone. Swimming and cycling can be excellent ways to build fitness and keep moving, yet because the water or bicycle supports much of the body, they generally provide less upright loading than walking. That difference is a description of the stimulus, not a verdict on the value of the activity. Enjoyment, access, pain, cardiovascular health and consistency matter too.
Balance is its own useful category

Strength and bone loading do not automatically make someone steady on their feet. Balance practice works on control: noticing where your body is, shifting weight, and adjusting when a surface or direction changes. A simple example might be standing near a stable counter and practising a narrow stance, if that is appropriate for you. Tai chi and some forms of dancing also challenge balance while involving movement. The practical reason to include this category is distinct from claims about bone density: steadier movement may help address fall risk, while bone-density measurements describe a different outcome. A program can include both, but one does not prove the other. Nor does a balance exercise need to look athletic to be purposeful; a safe, repeatable challenge matched to the person may be more useful than an impressive move performed without control.

Bone research often measures bone mineral density at particular sites, such as the hip or lumbar spine. Those measurements matter, but they are not a direct readout of strength, balance, or whether an individual will experience a fracture. Results also differ with participants, exercise design, duration and the bone site measured. A 2025 systematic review of resistance training in postmenopausal women reported improvements in bone mineral density at the lumbar spine, femoral neck and total hip, but not the trochanter; the authors also noted substantial variation across some results and a need for more high-quality trials [2]. This is evidence about a specific population and set of outcomes, not proof that a particular routine will produce the same change for every person. Useful conclusions should stay as specific as the evidence.
Why one activity rarely answers every question

A review of exercise guidance for people with osteoporosis treats resistance, impact and balance training as distinct elements, and emphasizes tailoring activity to individual health and characteristics [3]. That distinction helps explain why a person can be active yet still want to ask whether their routine includes progressive resistance, upright weight-bearing movement, or balance challenges. It also prevents a common overreach: assuming that a change in bone density proves improved balance, or that feeling stronger guarantees lower fracture risk. These are related areas of health, not interchangeable measures. Exercise may support several goals at once, but no single outcome should be used as shorthand for all the others. The most honest question is not “Which exercise builds bone best?” in the abstract; it is “Which movement qualities are relevant and appropriate for this person?”
A practical way to map your week

Try a short movement inventory before changing anything. Write down the activities you already do, then mark which ones involve (1) muscles working against resistance, (2) upright weight-bearing or impact, and (3) deliberate balance practice. An activity can earn more than one mark: a controlled step-up, for instance, uses body weight and challenges balance. Notice what is present and what is absent without treating the list as a scorecard. If you want to add resistance work and you have no medical restrictions, begin with movements you can control—such as sit-to-stands from a sturdy chair, a wall push-up, or a band row. Use a light load at first, move through a comfortable range, and stop if you develop sharp pain, dizziness or unusual symptoms. When a movement feels manageable, progress gradually by adjusting one feature, such as resistance or repetitions, rather than changing everything at once.

Impact is the category most likely to be misunderstood as a universal challenge to pursue. Higher-impact actions, including jumping, can be inappropriate for some people, particularly those with osteoporosis, low bone density, a prior fracture, pain, balance limitations or other health conditions. A lower-impact choice is not a failure; it may be the sensible way to stay active while getting advice or building capacity. If you have a diagnosis, have had a fracture, or are unsure what loading is safe, ask a health care professional who knows your circumstances before adding impact or increasing resistance. NIAMS specifically advises people with low bone density, osteoporosis or physical limitations to discuss safe activity with a health care provider [1]. Ask about the movements you want to do, not just whether exercise is allowed, and request alternatives if a suggested movement does not suit your body or setting.
Build a routine around roles, not promises

A balanced exercise week need not be elaborate. Keep activities you enjoy, identify a reasonable opportunity for progressive resistance, and consider whether upright movement and balance practice have a place. For one person, that might mean a walk, two brief strength sessions and supported balance work; another person may need a clinician or physical therapist to adapt the choices. These examples are categories, not a prescription or a guarantee of improved bone density. The more useful standard is whether the plan is safe, repeatable and connected to your goals. If you track progress, track the right thing: a lift becoming easier is evidence of a strength change, while a bone-density scan is a separate clinical measure. Bone health belongs in a broader picture of movement and wellbeing. Understanding what each activity asks of you makes that picture more accurate—and your next exercise decision more informed.
